query: What's actually the difference between a product cost and a period cost, and why does it matter?
key_points: product costs: tied to purchasing/producing inventory, capitalized as an asset;period costs: all other costs necessary to sustain the organization, expensed as incurred;the distinction determines when the cost hits the income statement

query: For a manufacturer, what three categories make up product costs?
key_points: three categories: direct materials, direct labor, manufacturing overhead;direct materials/labor = easily and economically traceable to the product;manufacturing overhead = all other indirect manufacturing costs

query: How does cost behavior differ between variable, fixed, and mixed costs?
key_points: variable cost: constant per unit, total changes with quantity;fixed cost: constant in total, per-unit cost changes with quantity;mixed cost: has both a variable and a fixed component

query: What exactly counts as manufacturing overhead, and what are some examples?
key_points: definition: indirect manufacturing costs that are neither direct material nor direct labor;examples of indirect materials: glue, nails, sandpaper;examples of indirect labor: supervisor's salary, quality control;other examples: rent, utilities, taxes on the production facility

query: Walk me through how costs flow through the inventory accounts in a job-order costing system.
key_points: four accounts: Raw Materials, Manufacturing Overhead, Work in Process, Finished Goods;direct materials/labor go into Work in Process; indirect materials/labor go into Manufacturing Overhead;overhead applied to WIP via predetermined rate;finished jobs move WIP -> Finished Goods -> Cost of Goods Sold upon sale

query: What kind of businesses typically use job-order costing instead of process costing?
key_points: job-order costing fits unique/custom products or services;example given: home construction company;costs are assigned directly to each individual job

query: How do you compute an organization-wide predetermined overhead rate?
key_points: formula: total estimated overhead / total estimated allocation base;common allocation bases: direct labor hours, machine hours, direct labor dollars, direct materials dollars;computed at the start of the period, applied throughout the year based on actual usage

query: When materials are requisitioned for production, how are direct materials and indirect materials recorded differently?
key_points: direct materials -> debited to Work in Process;indirect materials -> debited to Manufacturing Overhead;distinction is based on traceability to the specific product

query: What five factors does CVP analysis help managers understand the effect of on profit?
key_points: the five factors: selling prices, sales volume, unit variable costs, total fixed costs, mix of products sold;used to estimate the effect of changes in these factors on profit

query: Why is the contribution margin income statement so central to CVP analysis?
key_points: contribution margin income statement classifies costs by behavior (variable vs. fixed);traditional income statement classifies costs as product or period instead;this classification is essential for estimating how profit responds to changes in price, volume, costs, or mix

query: How do I calculate contribution margin per unit and the contribution margin ratio?
key_points: CM per unit = sales price per unit - variable cost per unit;CM ratio = contribution margin in dollars / sales revenue in dollars;both are used in break-even and target profit formulas

query: What's meant by 'cost structure' in a CVP context?
key_points: definition: the type and proportion of fixed vs. variable costs relative to total costs;central to what CVP analysis evaluates

query: What exactly is a master budget, and why does the sales budget come first?
key_points: master budget: collection of interrelated budgets covering sales, production, profit, financial position;sales budget goes first because it drives production, staffing, and facility decisions;budgets must be completed in a specific order because they feed into each other

query: What are the three main purposes budgeting serves for an organization?
key_points: three purposes: planning, controlling, performance evaluation;planning happens before the period, sets up operations;controlling sets targets/limits during the period;performance evaluation compares actual vs. budgeted results

query: Are budgets fixed once they're set at the start of the period?
key_points: budgets are estimates, not actual amounts, prepared before the period begins;they are frequently revised mid-period;reasons for revision: economic changes, sales demand shifts, other unforeseen factors

query: How does the budget actually get used for performance evaluation?
key_points: performance evaluation compares actual results to budgeted projections;used across departments/activities to check targets and spending limits;feedback used to correct inefficiencies or adjust future budget assumptions

query: What are standard costs, and why does a company set them?
key_points: standards = cost/revenue targets used for projections and performance evaluation;quantity standard: how much input is needed;price standard: how much each unit of input should cost;used both to project expenses and evaluate actual results

query: How is the total direct materials variance broken down?
key_points: total direct materials variance splits into: quantity variance and price variance;variance is caused by either a quantity difference or a price difference

query: What cost driver underlies all standard cost variance calculations?
key_points: actual production quantity is the cost driver used across all standard cost variances;the comparison is always: what should have been spent to produce actual output vs. what was actually spent

query: Can you walk through an example of computing a direct materials variance?
key_points: standard: 4.2 ft/unit at $0.50/ft;150,000 units produced -> standard quantity allowed = 630,000 ft, standard cost allowed = $315,000;actual: 600,000 ft costing $330,000;comparing standard vs. actual splits the variance into quantity and price components

query: How is ROI calculated, and what does it actually measure?
key_points: ROI formula: net operating income / average operating assets;measures both profitability and efficiency of asset use;usable at the organization, investment center, or project level

query: What's residual income, and how do you calculate it?
key_points: residual income = net operating income - (average operating assets x minimum required rate of return);positive = exceeds minimum required return; negative = falls short of it (but may still be profitable)

query: What's the relationship between ROI, profit margin, and asset turnover?
key_points: formula: ROI = profit margin x asset turnover;profit margin = profitability per sales dollar; asset turnover = efficiency of asset use in generating sales;shows how both dimensions combine into overall ROI

query: What's a downside of using residual income instead of ROI to evaluate a project?
key_points: residual income yields a dollar figure, not a percentage;doesn't reveal the exact return percentage above/below the minimum threshold;ROI is needed alongside it to get the actual percentage

query: In a make-or-buy decision, which costs should I actually consider relevant?
key_points: only relevant (avoidable) costs matter -- costs that differ between the make and buy alternatives;costs incurred regardless of the decision (e.g. existing overhead, a supervisor's regular salary) are irrelevant

query: How does the textbook define 'relevant costs' for differential decision making?
key_points: definition: relevant costs/benefits are those that differ between alternatives;differential decision making = analyzing only these relevant items to choose between alternatives

query: What four types of decisions does the differential decision making chapter cover?
key_points: four decision types: add/drop a segment, make or buy, special order, sell or process further;all use the same relevant-cost comparison approach

query: How do I calculate the payback period for an investment?
key_points: formula: payback period = investment required / annual net cash inflow;assumes constant annual net cash inflow;expressed in years

query: Why do I need to add back depreciation when using net operating income to find net cash inflow?
key_points: depreciation is a non-cash expense;payback method needs cash inflow, not accounting income;if net operating income is given, depreciation must be added back to get net cash inflow

query: What exactly counts as the 'required investment' in a payback period calculation?
key_points: required investment = project cost - trade-in/salvage value received;illustrated with the $12,000 purchase / $3,000 trade-in example, yielding $9,000 required investment

query: Is payback period meant to be the final decision-making tool, or something else?
key_points: payback period is typically a screening tool, not the final decision criterion;used to quickly filter competing projects against a payback threshold (e.g., 3-5 years);other tools (NPV, IRR) are needed for final selection

query: How can return on investment (ROI) be used to evaluate the profitability of a specific project, not just a whole business unit?
key_points: ROI isn't limited to evaluating whole organizations -- it can score a specific investment or project;formula: ROI = project's net operating income / project's cost;worked example: $3,000 net operating income / $27,000 cost = 11.1% ROI

query: What's an activity variance in flexible-budget analysis, and how does it isolate the effect of a change in sales volume alone?
key_points: activity variance = flexible budget amount - planning budget amount;isolates the effect of a change in sales volume alone, holding rates/prices constant;distinct from revenue and spending variances, which isolate price/cost effects at a fixed volume

query: What ratio would show whether a business unit is genuinely less efficient with its assets, rather than just a lower-margin business model?
key_points: profit margin ratio evaluates profitability but doesn't relate revenue to operating assets;asset turnover ratio isolates asset efficiency, independent of margin;comparing the two ratios across business units distinguishes 'lower margin business' from 'inefficient with its assets'

query: What ratio measures how efficiently a business unit generates sales from its operating assets, beyond its margin alone?
key_points: asset turnover ratio = how efficiently operating assets generate sales revenue;a stable margin doesn't guarantee stable asset efficiency;useful as a second check alongside margin, not a replacement for it

query: How can cost-volume-profit analysis be applied to individual customer segments instead of the whole business?
key_points: CVP analysis can be run at the segment level, not just for the whole organization;segment CVP requires a contribution-margin-format income statement for that segment;this is the same tool used for whole-organization CVP, just applied per-segment

query: In a differential cost decision, which costs are eliminated when a segment is dropped, and which persist regardless?
key_points: traceable fixed costs (tied specifically to the segment) are avoided/eliminated if the segment is dropped;common fixed costs (shared across multiple segments) persist regardless and are absorbed elsewhere;only traceable, avoidable costs are relevant to the drop decision

query: How does the textbook define relevant costs for a differential decision like cutting a specific cost bucket?
key_points: relevant costs/benefits = costs/benefits that differ between alternatives;differential decision making analyzes only these relevant items, ignoring costs that don't change;a cost's size relative to revenue doesn't establish relevance -- only whether it changes with the decision does

query: When a flexible-budget revenue variance is unfavorable, how should the manager investigate what caused it?
key_points: an unfavorable revenue variance should be traced to its specific, discoverable cause, not just reported as a shortfall;worked example: an unaccounted-for coupon-code promotion explained an unfavorable revenue variance;once the cause is known, the manager can take corrective action or update the budget formula if the cause is permanent

query: What method compares actual results to a flexible budget at the same sales volume to check whether a business met its revenue and cost targets?
key_points: revenue and spending variances = flexible budget vs. actual results, at the same sales volume;isolates whether targets were met on price/cost, separate from any pure volume effect;favorable if targets were met or beaten, unfavorable if not

query: Why are capital budgeting methods like NPV or payback period only as reliable as the estimates that feed them?
key_points: capital budgeting methods (NPV, payback, etc.) are practical tools, but their output is only as good as the input estimates;accuracy and quality of the projection data drives the reliability of the result;a sound method doesn't compensate for poor or already-wrong estimates

query: What's the most common error when calculating the effect of a change in sales quantity on net operating income?
key_points: most common CVP error: valuing a change in volume at sales price instead of contribution margin;only the contribution margin per unit (not full sales price) flows through to net operating income per unit sold, since fixed costs don't move with volume;matters directly when estimating how much a revenue-growth number should move EBITDA or net income

query: How does cost-volume-profit analysis decompose costs into variable and fixed components to test the effect of price or volume changes?
key_points: CVP analysis shows the effect on net operating income from changes in variable costs, fixed costs, selling price, and sales volume;applying it requires decomposing costs into their variable and fixed components, not just naming them;naming a cost-structure split isn't the same as running it through the CVP mechanics
